standard_prerequisites.name: Epimorphism between sets
standard_prerequisites.statement: A function f : A \to B between sets is an epimorphism when for every set C and every pair g, h : B \to C, g \circ f = h \circ f implies g = h.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the first of the three equivalent conditions.

standard_prerequisites.name: Mapping cone of a function
standard_prerequisites.statement: The mapping cone C_f is the pushout of f : A \to B with the map A \to \unit, with constructors t : C_f, \iota : B \to C_f and \alpha_1 : \prd{a:A} \iota(f(a)) = t.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the type whose contractibility is the second condition.

standard_prerequisites.name: Surjectivity as truncated fibres
standard_prerequisites.statement: f is surjective when \brck{\hfiber f b} is inhabited for every b : B.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the third condition and the hypothesis of the last implication.

standard_prerequisites.name: The dual statement for monomorphisms
standard_prerequisites.statement: The book's Lemma 10.1.1 characterises monomorphisms by several equivalent conditions, among them a statement about maps h with h \circ f being a homotopy of the same form.
standard_prerequisites.use: Its dual is applied to get the path gamma between the two pairs (source lines 216-217).

core_obligations: From f being an epimorphic function between sets, show the mapping cone C_f is contractible: exhibit t : C_f and prove \prd{x:C_f} x = t by induction on C_f, which reduces to data I_0 : \prd{b:B} \iota(b)=t and I_1 : \prd{a:A} \opp{\alpha_1(a)} \ct I_0(f(a)) = \refl t (source lines 197-210).

Package the two constructors \iota and the constant map as a pair in \sm{h:B\to C_f} \iota\circ f \htpy h \circ f and get a path gamma between the two pairs from the dual of the monomorphism lemma together with function extensionality, then extract I_0 and I_1 from gamma by the path characterisation of \Sigma-types (source lines 215-225).

Assuming C_f contractible, build a family P : C_f \to \prop by recursion, with P(t) \defeq \unit and P(\iota(b)) \defeq \brck{\hfiber f b}, the path to be given on the remaining constructor being supplied by the fact that \brck{\hfiber f{f(a)}} is an inhabited mere proposition hence equal to \unit (source lines 227-243).

Conclude surjectivity because contractibility of C_f makes all P(x) contractible, and finally derive the epimorphism property from surjectivity through the chain of equivalences from \prd{b:B} (g(b)=h(b)) to \prd{a:A} g(f(a))=h(f(a)) (source lines 245-257).

proof_roadmap.step: Epimorphism implies contractibility of the cone: reduce to the two induction data.
Get the path between the two pairs from the dual monomorphism lemma and read off I_0 and I_1.
Contractibility of the cone implies surjectivity, through the family P into propositions.
Surjectivity implies the epimorphism property by a chain of equivalences.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 172-195 (book Theorem 10.1.4): for a function f : A \to B between sets, being an epimorphism, having a contractible mapping cone and being surjective are equivalent. The statement contains no argument at all, and the proof (source lines 197-257) must supply three separate derivations. For the first it proves contractibility of the cone by induction on a higher inductive type, which requires producing both induction data, and these come from a path between two pairs in a \Sigma-type obtained by the dual of the book's monomorphism lemma together with function extensionality, after which the components must be extracted through the path characterisation of \Sigma-types. For the second it defines a family into the type of propositions by recursion on the cone, so it has to give a path between \brck{\hfiber f{f(a)}} and \unit, which is where the mere-proposition and inhabitedness arguments enter. For the third it produces the epimorphism property through a four-step chain of equivalences that moves the product over B into a product over A. Nothing of this is visible in the statement.
